subject: Coffee & Tea
title: What Is Oxidation?
description: A short lesson to help you apply What Is Oxidation?.

hook.text: Cut an apple and it turns brown. The same chemical process—oxidation—transforms tea leaves.

buildup.text: When tea leaves are bruised or rolled, enzymes react with oxygen, darkening the leaf and changing flavor.

discovery.text: Green tea is heated quickly to stop oxidation. Black tea is fully oxidized. Oolong stops somewhere between.

twist.text: Oxidation creates theaflavins and thearubigins—compounds that give black tea its amber color and malty taste.

climax.text: Controlling oxidation is the tea maker's core skill. Minutes of difference change the entire flavor profile.

punchline.text: Same leaf, different oxidation, different tea. Timing is flavor.

quiz.question: What chemical process distinguishes green tea from black tea?

details.summary: Oxidation is the enzymatic process where tea leaf cell walls break down and polyphenols react with oxygen, darkening the leaf and transforming flavor. Tea makers control oxidation by applying heat at precise moments, and this single variable largely determines whether tea becomes green, oolong, or.
details.whyItMatters: Oxidation is the most important concept in tea processing. It explains why leaves from the same bush can taste completely different.
takeaways: Oxidation darkens leaves and changes flavor compounds
Heat application stops oxidation at the desired level
Green tea is minimally oxidized; black tea is fully oxidized

faq.question: How do tea makers stop the oxidation process?
faq.answer: Heat denatures the enzymes responsible for oxidation. Chinese teas are typically pan-fired in a wok, while Japanese teas are steamed. The timing of this kill-green step determines the tea's final oxidation level and flavor character.

faq.question: Is oxidation the same as fermentation in tea?
faq.answer: No. Oxidation is an enzymatic reaction with oxygen. Fermentation involves microbes breaking down organic matter. True fermentation occurs only in dark teas like pu-erh. The tea industry historically confused the two terms, but modern usage distinguishes them.
